text: Diabetes occurs when the body cannot regulate blood glucose properly. This can happen when the body does not produce enough insulin or cannot use insulin effectively. Insulin helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells for energy.

The WHO describes type 1, type 2, and gestational diabetes. Type 1 involves the body no longer producing insulin. Type 2 involves the body not using insulin properly and gradually not producing enough. Gestational diabetes is elevated blood glucose during pregnancy that is above normal but below the criteria for diabetes outside pregnancy.

Possible symptoms include feeling very thirsty or hungry, frequent urination, extreme fatigue, blurred vision, and unexplained weight loss. Type 2 diabetes may have mild symptoms or no noticeable symptoms for years.
Persistently high blood glucose can damage the heart, kidneys, eyes, nerves, and blood vessels over time.
WHO says type 2 diabetes can often be prevented or delayed. Measures include regular physical activity, a healthy diet, maintaining a healthy body weight, and avoiding tobacco use.

WHO says diabetes management depends on the type of diabetes and may include healthy eating, regular physical activity, blood glucose monitoring, medication, support for self-management, management of other risk factors, and screening and treatment for complications.

Support for self-management can include education and psychosocial support. WHO describes effective diabetes care as long-term follow-up within primary health care, with referral to specialized services when needed.
WHO recommends asking a person living with diabetes what support would be helpful, listening without judgement, and avoiding comments about their lifestyle or diabetes management.
